Carter states: \"Two major sevenths I and IV\" (Ch12 p.117). This membership defines where maj7 naturally appears without alteration or borrowing in the diatonic seventh-chord taxonomy.", "source_principle_ids": ["bill-carter:complete-fingerstyle-jazz-guitar:cycle-voice-leading"], "source_work_id": "complete-fingerstyle-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "complete-fingerstyle-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 12 p.117"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "maj7", "function_role": "open-position-voicing", "narrative": "For physical playability on guitar, the third of the maj7 chord is displaced up an octave from its close-position location. Carter explains: \"the third of the chord has been moved an octave higher\" as a \"standard alternate configuration\" (Ch12 p.117).", "source_principle_ids": ["bill-carter:complete-fingerstyle-jazz-guitar:solo-arrangement"], "source_work_id": "complete-fingerstyle-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "complete-fingerstyle-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 12 p.117"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "maj7", "function_role": "cycle-voice-leading", "narrative": "When maj7 chords appear in cycle-of-fifths progressions, Carter prescribes tracking common tones held between adjacent chords while the remaining voices move by half step or whole step. He analyzes V7-to-I motion showing the tritone resolving inward and common tones maintained (Ch16 pp.155-157): \"If you think of harmonic movement as several moving voices rather than a glob of dots on a chord box grid, your arrangements and improvisations will be more airy, more interesting and less clunky.\"", "source_principle_ids": ["bill-carter:complete-fingerstyle-jazz-guitar:cycle-voice-leading"], "source_work_id": "complete-fingerstyle-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "complete-fingerstyle-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 16 pp.155-157"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "maj7", "function_role": "solo-arrangement-minimal-voicing", "narrative": "In solo fingerstyle arrangements, maj7 (and all chords) should be voiced as two or three notes so the melody can dominate. Carter states: \"Chords, for instance, are most often only two or three notes, and the melody is all-important\" (Ch18 p.169).", "source_principle_ids": ["bill-carter:complete-fingerstyle-jazz-guitar:solo-arrangement"], "source_work_id": "complete-fingerstyle-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "complete-fingerstyle-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 18 p.169"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "harmonic-family-membership", "narrative": "Exactly one dominant seventh chord is diatonic to any major key: the V. Carter specifies: \"dominant seventh defined with just root and third\" (Ch13 p.129). This minimal voicing communicates the dom7 function clearly while leaving textural space for the melody above.", "source_principle_ids": ["bill-carter:complete-fingerstyle-jazz-guitar:solo-arrangement", "bill-carter:complete-fingerstyle-jazz-guitar:cycle-voice-leading"], "source_work_id": "complete-fingerstyle-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "complete-fingerstyle-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 13 p.129"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "tritone-resolution", "narrative": "The tritone interval embedded in the dom7 resolves inward by half step to the root and third of the target I chord. He writes: \"the half step movement of the tritone interval here on beats one and three is more common than root movement. This is especially true if you are playing with a bass player who covers roots and fifths\" (Ch17 p.159).", "source_principle_ids": ["bill-carter:complete-fingerstyle-jazz-guitar:cycle-voice-leading"], "source_work_id": "complete-fingerstyle-jazz-guitar", "references": [{"source": "complete-fingerstyle-jazz-guitar", "citation": "chapter 17 p.159"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "tritone-substitution", "narrative": "Any dom7 chord may be replaced by the dominant seventh built a tritone away, since both chords share the same tritone interval. Carter notes: \"There is no explicitly stated root or fifth of the chord.
